question_technical: When an interest is declared, is it *managed* — i.e. does the member recuse?
title_technical: Do councillors step out when they declare a conflict?
objection: Declaring a conflict looks like disclosure theatre if the councillor who declares it goes on to vote anyway — a safeguard that only requires saying the words changes nothing in practice.
response: Disclosure is real, not cosmetic: declaring an interest measurably raises the chance a member steps out, and many of these declarations are lawful 'impartiality' interests the member is entitled to stay and vote on regardless. But that only clears the identify-and-disclose half of the safeguard — the *manage* half still breaks more often than it holds, since staying in the room and voting is still the more common outcome once an interest is declared.

question_technical: Did stepping out of serious conflicts change around external scrutiny?
title_technical: Did recusal compliance track the Authorised Inquiry?
objection: The apparent fall in recusal is just an artefact of composition — declarations shifted toward lawful 'impartiality' interests where the member is entitled to stay, so nothing about actual mandatory-conflict behaviour changed.
response: Impartiality declarations did increase substantially, so part of the composition shift is real. But the decline shows up *within* the must-leave categories too, not only in the mix between them — proximity-conflict recusal fell after the period of heightened external scrutiny, not just its share of all declarations. Financial conflicts are too rare on their own to show a trend either way, so the within-category evidence rests on the proximity category, not the financial one.

question_technical: How often does council depart from the officer recommendation?
title_technical: Does the chamber decide, or ratify its officers?
objection: If officers get their way almost every time, 'debate' is theatre and the substantive decision is really made upstream, in whoever writes the recommendation — the council vote is a formality.
response: Exceptions are a genuine minority, not an absent check: every recorded departure from an officer recommendation is listed and inspectable here, not buried inside an otherwise-unanimous-looking vote. Divergence is rare, but it is real, and it is auditable rather than assumed.

question_technical: On contested votes, how unequal is who actually wins — and is it accountable?
title_technical: Does consensus hide a power hierarchy?
objection: However contested a vote looks on paper, the same handful of councillors win most of the time, so 'debate' is theatre for a fixed majority — some members are consistently on the losing side more often than the winning one.
response: That spread resets every election rather than calcifying around one clique — the term-by-term picture shows real churn in who ends up on top. And dissent is not merely symbolic: a meaningful share of contested motions actually fail, so objecting carries real leverage, not just recorded protest.

question_technical: What share of decided items is confidential, and is it rising?
title_technical: How much business is taken behind closed doors?
objection: A spike in confidential business coinciding with a period of active external scrutiny looks like the opposite of transparency — hiding more precisely when outsiders were watching closest.
response: The long-run baseline is a genuinely open record, and a period of active external scrutiny legitimately generates confidential business — legal advice and personnel matters under active investigation — so some rise in those years is expected, and it reverted once scrutiny ended. That concedes the pattern is not baseline behaviour. What it still raises is the *scale* of the spike and its *timing* relative to the scrutiny period: read in the round, this reads as a transparent council that went unusually quiet during a period of active scrutiny, not a habitually secretive one.

question_technical: Do confidential tenders carry higher dollar values than open ones?
title_technical: Are the redacted tenders the bigger contracts?
objection: The confidential-tender sample here is small, and most confidential tenders don't even record a dollar figure at all — a pattern built on so few priced observations could easily be noise, not a real difference in contract size.
response: The small sample is why this is stated as directional rather than definitive. But the gap this measure can't see cuts the other way: tenders missing a recorded amount are excluded from the comparison entirely, and that missingness biases toward understating any real difference, not manufacturing one — so a small but real sample is, if anything, an undersell of the true gap. Confidentiality on a tender is often lawful in its own right, so this is a visibility concern rather than evidence of impropriety.

question_technical: What share of public questions are deferred rather than answered in the meeting, over time?
title_technical: Are residents' questions answered, or quietly 'taken on notice'?
objection: Most public questions are still answered in the meeting — the great majority get a live answer, so this isn't really a responsiveness problem.
response: What matters is the shift, not the level: deferral rose substantially once the council came under a period of heightened external scrutiny and never fully returned to its earlier baseline — and the measure, if anything, understates that shift. Part of the single-year peak is a remote-meeting artefact (meetings went online and complex questions were reasonably answered in writing), but the rise began before the remote period and persisted well after it ended, so a temporary shift to remote meetings doesn't carry the trend on its own. 'Taken on notice' is lawful and often appropriate for complex questions, so this reads as a responsiveness concern, not impropriety.
